title: Exclude graphics cards at the prompt, and remove what the omission already produced
body:
All three slices of `docs/plans/oracle/claim-store-hygiene.md`, in the order the plan sets: the root cause first, then the corpus, then the document. Replaces #210, which the review gate blocked correctly for borrowing an unrelated plan's slug and for fixing a symptom with no permanent check.

**Slice 1 — the prompt.** `prompts/extract-claims.md` told the model to skip claims about a CPU, a chipset in general, or the industry, and never mentioned graphics cards. Buildzoid reviews those too, so a GPU PCB breakdown produced dozens of well-formed, correctly-categorised, verbatim-quoted claims about a product this project is not about — 35 unambiguous ones in a corpus of 2771. **ESC-29** records it, and records the real gap: the prompt is a committed artifact that no gate reads.

The exclusion is now a RULE rather than a list — *"a claim about anything that is not a motherboard is not a claim about a board"* — with CPUs, chipsets, the industry and graphics cards as its examples rather than its extent. That is ESC-29's third candidate and the cheapest: an enumeration only ever decides the members somebody thought of. The counterweight sits in the same place, because it is the half that can be got wrong expensively: **a video about a graphics card still contains claims about motherboards.** He discusses the board he is testing on. It is the subject of the SENTENCE that decides, never the subject of the video.

**Slice 2 — the corpus.** `scripts/drop-gpu-claims.py` implements the three-signal rule the plan's first Uncertainty rules on. Neither cheap signal works alone: dropping by video destroys the motherboard claims GPU videos contain, and dropping by board name misfires the other way, since `MSI 970 Gaming Krait` is a motherboard.

**The owner's ruling is mechanical here, not a promise in a docstring.** Given in chat twice, the second time unprompted — *"it is way more important to include motherboards than to exclude gpus"*. So two guards: a claim from a video titled `mobo`/`motherboard`/`mainboard` is never dropped, and that check never consults the GPU rules, so widening a regex cannot defeat it; and the script **refuses to write** when the rule matches more than 5% of the store, because a script that deletes a third of the corpus and reports it cheerfully is indistinguishable, in its output, from one that worked.

Measured against the pre-cleanup store: **35 of 2771, 1.26%, none from a motherboard-titled video.** All 35 were read individually rather than sampled — the ruling makes a sample insufficient — and every one names a graphics card, a GPU model number or card-specific hardware. Reporting is the default, `--apply` is required to write, the original is kept at `claims.jsonl.bak`, and a second run finds nothing.

**R27 is not touched.** It governs the raw model output under `data/claims/batch-<n>/`, written before anything parses it. The store is derived, and this is a committed script rather than a hand edit, so it is reproducible and auditable.

**Slice 3 — the document.** `docs/reading-the-claims.md`, for whoever reads the store next with no memory of how it got there. The fields, the three closed vocabularies, and the fact that `video_id` plus `timestamp_seconds` is a URL so every claim is checkable in one click — a 40-claim random audit found 40 of 40 snippets present verbatim in their source transcript. Most of it is the four ways the data misleads a careless reader, including that slice 2 deliberately did NOT remove every graphics-card claim and roughly 90 remain.

**Both test suites were written blind**, by two agents that could not see this implementation, and both landed as commits BEFORE it — `blind-tests.sh` reports every blind-written test unmodified since its authoring commit. **243 cases.** The prompt's five fail against the old wording in both directions: one fires on an over-correcting prompt that would discard a whole GPU video, which is the error the owner ruled against. The script's 138 include **62 aimed at over-deletion**, and were mutation-tested against a throwaway reference — removing the title-absolute rule fails 12, removing the board-token keep-rule fails 26, and turning the ceiling's `>` into `>=` fails exactly the three boundary cases.

**No disagreement at assembly:** 138 of 138 and 5 of 5 passed against this implementation on the first run.

Ran locally: `blind-tests.sh`, `escape-refs.sh`, `acceptance-criteria.sh`, `owner-authored.sh`, ruff, format, mypy, **2097 passed**.
